title: Neuron decay and regeneration
content_html:
Neuron decay and regeneration

Most neurons do not regenerate, but they also don’t simply “decay” like other cells - instead, they can last a lifetime while undergoing continual molecular renewal and synaptic remodeling. Most neurons in the cerebral cortex, hippocampus, and cerebellum are formed during early development and persist for decades - sometimes for the entire lifespan. These neurons are post-mitotic, meaning they don’t divide once mature, but despite this, they maintain themselves through molecular repair and protein turnover, replacing damaged components without dividing the cell itself. The cell remains, but its contents are constantly renewed; a 60-year-old neuron may contain proteins that are only days old.

Certain brain regions do continue to generate new neurons - a process called adult neurogenesis.

Brain Region Function Notes
Hippocampus (dentate gyrus) Memory formation, pattern separation New neurons integrate into existing circuits and may aid learning.
Subventricular zone (near lateral ventricles) Olfactory processing In rodents this is significant; in humans, much less so.

Even though neurons rarely die, they accumulate wear and tear, through oxidative stress, protein aggregation, and DNA damage contribute to age-related decline. Neurons rely on glial cells (especially astrocytes and microglia) for metabolic support, debris clearance, and inflammation control. Synapses (connections) are constantly pruned and rebuilt, allowing adaptive rewiring without neuron loss. Think of the brain less as a static wiring diagram, and more as a living city: buildings (neurons) remain, but streets, lights, and utilities (synapses and molecules) are constantly replaced.

Memory depends on the persistence of change within matter that itself renews. Even as molecules turnover, structural and synaptic patterns endure, encoding memories through relative arrangement, not material permanence. The brain forgets chemically, but remembers structurally; the pattern - not the particle - is what survives.
